result:
The rain doesn't fall here anymore. It used to, in long silver sheets that turned the gutters into rivers and made every window look like it was crying. Now the sky is just this pale, exhausted thing that hangs over the city like a sheet that's been washed too many times. Everything feels reused. Even the light.

I keep thinking about the woman on the train yesterday. She was maybe sixty, maybe a hundred and sixty. Hard to tell anymore. She had one of those faces that looks like it was carved by someone who was angry at marble. Sharp cheekbones, eyes like two small black stones someone forgot to polish. She was reading a book with no title on the spine, and every few pages she'd lick her finger with this strange deliberate slowness, like she was tasting the paper for poison.

When she caught me staring, she didn't look away. Most people do. She just stared back until I felt my face get hot, until I could feel my own pulse in my teeth. Then she smiled. Not a nice smile. The kind of smile that knows exactly what your childhood nightmares smelled like.

"You see them too," she said. Her voice was quiet but it cut through the train noise like a scalpel through wet paper. "The ones who aren't breathing right."

I didn't answer. What do you say to that?

She leaned forward. I could smell her perfume—something like burnt sugar and old churches. "They're getting bolder. Last week one sat next to me for six stops. Kept trying to borrow my face. I told it no. They don't like that."

The train stopped. She stood up, all bones and silk and ancient mischief, and as she passed me she pressed something into my hand. It was warm. Too warm.

"Don't feed them your memories," she whispered. "They get fat on those."

Then she was gone. The thing in my hand was a tooth. Human. Perfect. With a tiny symbol carved into it that hurt to look at directly.

I should have thrown it away. Instead I put it in my pocket like a lunatic.

That's the thing about this city now. Everything feels like it's leaning. Like the buildings are listening. Like the pigeons have opinions. I walk past the same café every morning and the barista always has the same burn on his left wrist shaped like South America and he always says "the usual?" even though I've never been there before in my life. The coffee is always perfect. Too perfect. Like it knows what I want better than I do.

Last night I dreamed I was underwater but I could breathe. There were people down there having a dinner party. They were all me. Different ages. The seven-year-old version kept trying to tell me something but every time he opened his mouth, bubbles came out that turned into tiny screaming faces before floating away. The old man version of me just kept cutting his steak very methodically, even though it was bleeding light.

I woke up with the tooth in my fist. It had gotten hotter. Almost burning.

This morning I went back to the train station. I don't know why. The trains weren't running. There was just this one car sitting on the tracks with all its lights on, doors open, completely empty except for one thing.

A book. The same one the woman had been reading.

I picked it up.

The pages were blank except for the very center. There, in handwriting that looked exactly like mine but somehow older, were three words:

YOU ALREADY DID

I don't know what that means. I don't want to know what that means.

But I keep hearing breathing behind me when I'm alone. Not my breathing. Something with too many lungs.

The tooth is in my pocket right now. It's singing.

I think I might be running out of time to be afraid.

The sky just flickered. Like a bad bulb.

Anyway. That's what came to me.

All 487 words of it. The rest is just silence wearing my face.
